title: Speech
hookLine: precept four: refrain from false speech
last: SEXUAL CONDUCT — NO HARM IN LOVE.

lines: A FATHER, A BOY, A DIPPER.
cards: I'm five minutes away, said from the couch. I love it, said about the sweater. Sorry, just saw this, about a text that arrived three hours ago.
Small untrue things, the kind that grease the day. Nobody gets hurt, goes the thinking.
The fourth precept is about exactly these words, and the Pali Canon teaches it with a vivid scene: a father, a small boy, and a dipper of water.

teach.b: In Pali: Musavada veramani sikkhapadam samadiyami. I undertake the training rule to refrain from false speech. Musa means false; vada, speech.
Now the story. The Buddha's son, Rahula, had joined the order as a boy. One evening the Buddha visited him, and Rahula set out water for his feet.

teach.h: THE DIPPER: A LITTLE WATER LEFT.
teach.b: The Buddha washed, left a little water in the dipper, and asked: do you see this small amount? That's how little of the spiritual life is in someone who isn't ashamed to tell a deliberate lie.
He tossed the water out: that's how easily it's thrown away. He turned the dipper upside down: that's how it's overturned. He turned it back, empty: that's how empty it is.
Then something gentle and practical: don't tell a lie, even as a joke.
Before you act or speak, look, the way you'd look in a mirror, and ask whether it will harm anyone. Another discourse adds the other half.

Asked whether he ever said unwelcome things, the Buddha pointed to a baby on a prince's lap. If the child had a stick or a stone in its mouth, you'd take it out, even if it drew a little blood, out of compassion.

teach.h: TRUE, HELPFUL, AT THE RIGHT TIME.
teach.b: He speaks what is true and helpful, he said, and he knows the right time to say it.
So the precept isn't permission to be brutal. It's truth, with care about timing and kindness. The small lie trades a moment of comfort for a little less trust.
The precept trains the other trade.

how: Buddhists recite the fourth precept, to refrain from false speech, with the other four, and many teachers pair it with the fuller idea of right speech: true, helpful, kind and well timed.

o: staying silent so you never say a wrong word
refraining from false words, even small ones
saying every true thing the moment you think it

games.q: who did what in today's teaching — tap the pairs.
p: left a little water in the dipper
set out water for his father's feet
look before you speak or act
take it out, even if it hurts

s: the Buddha told Rahula not to lie even as a joke
that's in the discourse to Rahula, right after the dipper.
the fourth precept means saying every true thing, whenever you think it
the Buddha spoke what was true and helpful, and knew the right time.

games.q: a baby on your lap has put a sharp stone in its mouth. taking it out will make the baby cry. what do you do?
o: take it out, gently, even if it hurts.
games.why: the Buddha used this picture for hard truths: you take it out, out of compassion, and you choose the right moment.

practice: Think back over the last day and find one small untrue thing you said; no big confession, just notice what it was protecting: your comfort, their feelings, your image.
Then picture that moment and imagine the true version, said kindly. Hear how it sounds; maybe it's easier than you thought.

wordCard.voice: Speech. The fourth precept: a training to refrain from false speech, and to say what's true and helpful, at the right time.

orig.note: Pali: false speech (musa, false + vada, speech); the fourth precept is to refrain from it.

carryVoice: Your line: say what's true. True, helpful, and at the right time. That's day one hundred twenty-seven.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 61 (Ambalatthika Rahulovada Sutta), the dipper and the mirror
Majjhima Nikaya 58 (Abhayarajakumara Sutta), the baby with a stick in its mouth
